The Data Bunker (d-bunker)

Data Tsunami
It has been years since governments and big tech stopped sulfur injection into the atmosphere, yet their control over humanity has only strengthened. Libraries were once repositories of information - a physically confined space within which information existed. Now, information is more readily available than ever causing an information overload, but how much of this information can we trust?

During humanity’s struggle with SAI’s adverse effects, a group of Meta investors and technopreneurs opened their bunkers to those less fortunate, ultimately expanding into the utopian city Hyperion. Governed by technology, neural augmentation and bio-tech were introduced as a means of connection in the city, enabling easy data access, and mental enhancement. However, content absorption has reached an extreme. Media streams every waking second of a person’s day, and VR lenses cause people to escape to a false reality. Individual thoughts begin ceasing to exist, neural data chips monitor all actions, and people lose track of what is real and what is not.

Shelter from the Digital Storm
A group of data scientists began trying to develop neural blocking technology as a challenge, attempting the opposite of their current work - it took just one day of disconnection from their media streams to realize how cluttered, influenced and dysfunctional the information they store in their brains was. In resistance, they retreated to an abandoned bunker hidden under fallen boulders, creating the Data Bunker.

The Data Bunker is designed not purely to accumulate information but to filter, organize, and “clean” information. Aiming to combat the effects of information overload and constant media bombardment, the library allows its visitors to escape AI-driven information, rediscover their individuality and nurture cognitive flexibility without the interference of big tech and government propaganda. Run by a set of steadfast “data-librarians”, information is constantly being entered, parsed, filtered, and de-biased in their protected internal chambers.

Reaching for Mental Liberation
Librarians are active fact checkers, trained to curate and retain valuable knowledge while discarding trivial or misleading information for visitors. Silent zones with noise-canceling environments and meditation pods allow for deep mental detoxification. In these pods, people can disconnect from their chips, storing encrypted thoughts and ideas safe from monitoring.

The librarians are continuously working towards updating the library’s main collection, the DataPulse map – a comprehensive information chamber combining all available sources, highlighting falsehoods, and holographically displaying visitors internal echo chamber on the map. At the end of the neural cleansing process, visitors enter the chamber - their lenses enable them to visualize their personal filter bubble in a bio-metrically decided color, while the surrounding information map is dull. Visitors can move around and select new “branches” of data to expand their thinking. The colors grow increasingly vibrant, and their “bubble” grows every time they seek out something new. While entry benefits them by decluttering their brains and regaining their individuality, visitors risk a brutal discovery of false beliefs, deeply biased thinking, or a realization of their fabricated reality.

The library is an act of resistance against forces of control and homogenization. By harnessing neurotechnology, it empowers individuals to reclaim sovereignty over their thoughts, resisting the subtle influences of manipulation.

The Biophilia Library

In the distant future, the Earth’s surface has become increasingly harsh due to the extreme effects of climate change. Initial attempts to stabilize global temperatures, such as Stratospheric Aerosol Injection (SAI), led to severe and unpredictable environmental consequences. The once rich and diverse ecosystems of the planet have been decimated, leaving barren landscapes where forests and biodiversity hotspots once flourished.

Amidst this turmoil, humanity found refuge in underground cities. These subterranean habitats provided stability and security, but the inhabitants longed for the natural beauty and tranquility of the surface. The harsh and unfamiliar underground environment caused significant stress and anxiety, as people struggled with the loss of their connection to nature—a connection that has been proven to be vital for mental health and well-being. To address this need, the Biophilia Library was established deep within one of these underground cities.

The Biophilia Library is no ordinary repository. It houses the genetic blueprints and seeds of plant species that once thrived on the surface. These genetic materials are not just stored but are genetically engineered and integrated into the roots of plants that are grown inside there.

Researchers have found that spending time in nature or even viewing natural scenes can reduce mental fatigue and improve concentration, a concept known as biophilia. The Biophilia Library leverages this principle to help the underground community reconnect with nature. Its primary mission is to preserve genetic information in the form of biological material and to provide a sanctuary where people can experience the restorative effects of nature.

Humans developed a revolutionary method to genetically engineer and encode data directly into the DNA of plants, allowing for efficient storage and retrieval of information whenever needed. The data stored within these plants include comprehensive genetic blueprints that can be used for future reforestation and ecosystem restoration. This method of storage is energy-efficient, relying on the natural process of photosynthesis. As long as the plants remain alive, the genetic data stays intact, making the library a self-sustaining and ever-growing repository.

The library’s collection includes both ancient species that once thrived on Earth and new hybrid species adapted to the changing conditions. These plants serve as a living record of Earth’s botanical history and its evolutionary adaptations to climate change.

The unique aspect of the Biophilia Library is its symbiotic relationship with its human caretakers. The library’s growth and expansion are guided by the plants themselves. As plants grow and spread, they indicate which parts of the cave are stable and suitable for further development. This natural guidance ensures that the library’s expansion is safe and sustainable. The plants essentially map out habitable areas, providing humans with a guaranteed safety.

This symbiotic relationship extends to the library’s capacity for data storage. As plants grow, they increase the library’s storage capacity, allowing for continuous accumulation of genetic information. This natural expansion ensures that the library remains a dynamic and evolving institution, always ready to adapt to the changing needs of its environment.

In addition to its role as a conservation center, the Biophilia Library offers practical resources for underground living. Visitors can borrow seeds embedded with genetic information to grow plants in their own homes, provided these plants can thrive in subterranean conditions. The library also supplies specially formulated soil to support the growth of these plants, ensuring that everyone has the opportunity to cultivate their own piece of nature. However, borrowing seeds of plants that will not survive underground is not permitted.
